title: One-Dimensional Motion
learning_goal: Analyze one-dimensional motion using distance, displacement, speed, velocity, reference frames, and acceleration.

concept_cards.title: Distance vs. displacement
concept_cards.content: Distance is the total path traveled. Displacement is the signed change in position from start to finish.

concept_cards.title: Speed vs. velocity
concept_cards.content: Speed describes how fast. Velocity describes how fast and in what direction. The sign of velocity tells direction in one-dimensional motion.

concept_cards.title: Reference frames
concept_cards.content: Motion is always described relative to a reference point or coordinate system. A passenger can be at rest relative to a car but moving relative to the road.

concept_cards.title: Acceleration
concept_cards.content: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. An object accelerates when velocity changes in magnitude or direction.

worked_examples.prompt: A runner moves from x = 2 m to x = 14 m in 4 s. Find the average velocity.

solution_steps.explanation: The positive sign means motion in the positive direction.

worked_examples.prompt: A cart moves from x = 9 m to x = −3 m in 6 s. Find the average velocity.

solution_steps.explanation: Final position minus initial position gives a negative displacement.
Divide signed displacement by elapsed time.
The negative sign means motion in the negative direction.

worked_examples.prompt: A train changes velocity from 4 m/s to 16 m/s in 6 s. Find the average acceleration.

solution_steps.explanation: Divide velocity change by elapsed time.
Velocity increases by 2 m/s each second on average.

guided_practice.prompt: A cart moves from x = 10 m to x = 2 m in 4 s. What is its average velocity?
hint_steps: Find displacement first: final position minus initial position.
Compute 2 − 10 and keep the negative sign.
Divide the signed displacement by 4 s.
guided_practice.alternate_explanation: Use the number line: the cart moves 8 m toward smaller x-values, so its displacement is negative before you divide by time.

similar_problem.prompt: A robot moves from x = 6 m to x = −6 m in 6 s. What is its average velocity?

guided_practice.prompt: A cyclist moves from x = −4 m to x = 20 m in 6 s. What is the average velocity?
guided_practice.alternate_explanation: Picture the trip in two parts: from −4 m to zero is 4 m to the right, and from zero to 20 m is another 20 m to the right. The total displacement is therefore +24 m. Average velocity tells us the signed change in position per second over the whole trip; it does not mean the cyclist kept the same velocity at every instant.
alternate_explanation_steps: Identify the starting position xᵢ = −4 m, ending position x_f = 20 m, and elapsed time Δt = 6 s.
Find displacement: Δx = x_f − xᵢ = 20 − (−4) = 20 + 4 = +24 m. Subtracting a negative adds its magnitude.
Use average velocity = displacement ÷ elapsed time: v_avg = (+24 m) ÷ (6 s) = +4 m/s.
The positive sign means motion toward increasing x, to the right on the diagram. The answer is 4 meters per second to the right.
Check: (4 m/s)(6 s) = 24 m, and −4 m + 24 m = 20 m, the stated final position.

similar_problem.prompt: A runner moves from x = −5 m to x = 15 m in 5 s. What is the average velocity?

guided_practice.prompt: A car's velocity changes from 3 m/s to 15 m/s in 4 s. What is its average acceleration?
hint_steps: Find the change in velocity first.
Divide the velocity change by 4 s.
guided_practice.alternate_explanation: Read the velocity-time change as rise over run: velocity rises by 12 m/s over 4 seconds.

similar_problem.prompt: A scooter changes velocity from 2 m/s to 12 m/s in 5 s. What is its average acceleration?

independent_practice.prompt: A car moves from x = 5 m to x = 29 m in 8 s. What is its average velocity?
independent_practice.alternate_explanation: The car changes position by 24 m over 8 s, so average velocity is the position change per second.

similar_problem.prompt: A bus moves from x = 4 m to x = 28 m in 6 s. What is its average velocity?

independent_practice.prompt: A student walks from x = 12 m to x = −6 m in 9 s. What is the average velocity?
hint_steps: Final position is less than initial position.
independent_practice.alternate_explanation: The student moves 18 m in the negative direction over 9 seconds.

similar_problem.prompt: A drone moves from x = 10 m to x = −5 m in 5 s. What is its average velocity?

independent_practice.prompt: A train has an initial velocity of 4 m/s and reaches 16 m/s in 6 s. What is its average acceleration?
hint_steps: Use change in velocity divided by elapsed time.
independent_practice.alternate_explanation: Velocity gains 12 m/s over 6 s, which is an average gain of 2 m/s each second.

similar_problem.prompt: A bicycle changes velocity from 5 m/s to 14 m/s in 3 s. What is its average acceleration?

independent_practice.prompt: A runner travels 30 m east, then 12 m west, in a total time of 6 s. Take east as positive. What is the runner's average velocity?
hint_steps: Average velocity uses displacement, not total distance.
Divide the net displacement by 6 s.
independent_practice.alternate_explanation: Draw the trip on a number line. Ending 18 m east of the start matters for velocity; the 42 m total path matters for distance.

similar_problem.prompt: A hiker walks 20 m east and 8 m west in 4 s. What is the average velocity?

conceptual_questions.prompt: A runner returns to the starting point after a trip. Explain why average velocity can be zero while average speed is positive.
expected_ideas: Net displacement is zero because final and initial positions are equal.
Average velocity uses displacement divided by elapsed time; average speed uses total path length divided by elapsed time.
misconceptions: Returning to the start means no distance was traveled.
conceptual_questions.follow_up: Which quantity uses the path and which uses only the endpoints?

conceptual_questions.prompt: A car moves in the negative direction and has positive acceleration. Explain whether it is initially speeding up or slowing down.
expected_ideas: Velocity and acceleration initially have opposite signs.
Speed initially decreases until velocity reaches zero; continued positive acceleration can then increase speed in the positive direction.
conceptual_questions.follow_up: What happens to a negative velocity when positive changes are added?
